strengths: Well-motivated identification of outcome-agnostic feature learning as a fundamental limitation of SpecIV, with clear intuition and formal characterization of misalignment scenarios

Theoretically sound framework: comprehensive non-asymptotic error bounds (Theorem 1), elegant connection to augmented operator SVD (Proposition 1), and rigorous perturbation analysis showing when augmentation helps (Theorem 4, spectral gap γ_d(δ))
Thorough experimental validation including controlled synthetic experiments, semi-synthetic dSprites with novel h_new benchmark, and off-policy evaluation demonstrating broader applicability

Honest treatment of limitations: acknowledges rank-one restriction, unresolved δ selection problem, gap between theory/practice, and provides multiple selection heuristics with discussion of their limitations
Technical rigor in proofs: appropriate application of Wedin perturbation theory, careful concentration arguments, clear separation of approximation and statistical error
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: core contribution reduces to adding outcome-aware regularization term; while effective, the conceptual innovation is limited and the modification is relatively straightforward

Significant practical limitation of rank-one perturbations: full theory only covers rank-1, extensions to higher rank acknowledged as incomplete (Section E), and preliminary rank-2 results show minimal additional benefit

Unresolved hyperparameter selection: introduces new δ parameter requiring tuning; Section 6.4 proposes heuristics without theoretical guarantees; Section D.8 explicitly states 'theoretical justification...remains elusive'—undermines claim of automatic robustness

Modest empirical improvements: dSprites h_old shows ~20% gains over baseline (which already works well); h_new approximately matches DFIV without dramatic outperformance; OPE shows no uniform improvement across tasks (Figure 10)

Gap between theory and practice: assumes compact T but OPE involves non-compact operators; optimality gap E_d(θ,ω,δ) unbounded (acknowledged as open problem); complex condition (Eq. 15) restricts Theorem 4 applicability; sub-Gaussian assumptions may not hold generally

Incomplete failure mode characterization: unclear how robust to δ misspecification (Figure 2 shows degradation but lacks analysis); 'bad scenario' analysis assumes known partition N—how to identify in practice; limited guidance on when augmentation is most beneficial
Computational efficiency unaddressed: no timing comparisons, overhead of ω optimization not discussed, high-dimensional scaling unclear

Practical utility of Proposition 2: alignment estimation requires fitted T̂_δ from finite samples; Figure 4 shows estimated alignment doesn't perfectly track performance; limited error analysis in finite-sample regime

strengths: Clear identification and principled solution to a real limitation of spectral IV methods (outcome-agnostic features)
Elegant operator-theoretic framework with Proposition 1 cleanly connecting augmented loss to SVD approximation
Comprehensive non-asymptotic theory: Theorem 1 provides high-probability bounds improving on prior results, and Theorem 4 carefully characterizes good/bad scenarios using perturbation theory
Extensive experimental validation across multiple domains (synthetic, dSprites with new hnew benchmark, OPE) demonstrating consistent improvements in misaligned regimes
Rigorous mathematical development: proper use of Wedin sin-Θ theorem, concentration inequalities, and careful error decomposition into signal/noise/gap components
Honest treatment of practical limitations with multiple δ selection strategies discussed (loss balancing, alignment estimation, cross-validation)
Strong reproducibility: detailed protocols, hyperparameter grids, architecture specifications in appendix
Thoughtful extension to higher-rank perturbations and applicability beyond standard IV (e.g., to OPE in RL)
weaknesses: Hyperparameter δ selection lacks principled theory: while three heuristics are proposed, none has full theoretical justification; Section D.8 shows theoretical issues with stage-2 loss selection; this is a significant practical barrier to deployment
Optimality gap Ed(θ,ω,δ) in Eq. (7) depends on DNN generalization bounds which are 'an open problem in its own right'—end-to-end theoretical guarantees incomplete

Rank-one augmentation limitation: current approach only incorporates E[Y|Z]; extension to higher ranks deferred for 'future work'; preliminary rank-2 results (Figure 14) don't show substantial additional gains
Sample complexity requirement n ≥ 16dρ²log²(4d/τ)c⁻² could be stringent when c⁻² is large under ill-posedness; limited discussion of manifestation in experiments

OPE experiments show mixed results (Figures 9-11): no method uniformly dominates across tasks; AugSpecIV outperforms SpecIV on Cartpole but underperforms on Mountain Car, weakening practical motivation
Limited guidance on when practitioners should expect spectral misalignment a priori, and how to detect it without solving the problem first
Main text dense with complex results; good scenario receives less attention despite being arguably more common; unclear exposition of when/how to use the framework
Restricted to compact operators (Assumption 1) and sub-Gaussian distributions (Assumption 4); OPE required non-standard iterative workaround due to non-compactness

strengths: Well-motivated problem identification with clear illustration of spectral misalignment and its consequences for outcome-agnostic methods
Elegant theoretical framework using augmented operators with clean characterization (Proposition 4.1) connecting contrastive loss to truncated SVD of T_δ
Comprehensive non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees (Theorem 5.1) improving on prior work (Chen & Christensen 2018) with high-probability bounds
Sophisticated perturbation analysis properly relating singular subspaces of augmented operator T_δ back to original T using Wedin sin-Θ theorem
Detailed error decomposition (Theorem C.6) characterizing both well-aligned ('good') and misaligned ('bad') scenarios with explicit dependence on spectral gap and noise
Novel connection between population contrastive excess loss and operator optimality gap (Proposition A.4) applicable even to standard SpecIV
Comprehensive experimental validation across synthetic, vision (dSprites), and reinforcement learning (OPE) domains with controlled parameters
Well-designed new dSprites benchmark (h_new) specifically targeting spectral misalignment as ground truth
Extensive experimental protocols and implementation details enabling reproducibility
Principled treatment of practical considerations (Section 6.4) exploring multiple δ-selection strategies
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 5.1 assumes learned features are obtained but doesn't control how well empirical DNN training minimizes the empirical augmented loss; authors acknowledge that proving Δ_δ→0 via optimization requires architecture-specific analysis left for future work

Fundamental unresolved issue: δ hyperparameter selection remains heuristic despite extensive discussion; no theoretical guidance provided; three proposed strategies (alignment estimation, loss balancing, second-stage minimization) all post-hoc; alignment estimator has numerical stability issues when ‖ω_δ‖→1

Limited practical improvements on standard benchmarks: only ~20% improvement over SpecIV on well-aligned original dSprites (h_old); substantial improvements concentrated on newly designed h_new benchmark; unclear when spectral misalignment actually occurs in real applications

Rank-1 augmentation limitation: theoretical results formally cover only scalar δ; higher-rank extension discussed in Section F but not analyzed theoretically, limiting applicability to problems requiring richer outcome representation
Mixed OPE experimental results: Section 6.3 states 'no OPE method performed uniformly well across all tasks'; method's advantage over baselines not clear in this application domain

Experimental design fairness concerns: different architectures used for DFIV comparisons (reduced features 32→16, GeLU vs ReLU); authors note DFIV performed 'slightly worse' than expected, raising questions about equal hyperparameter tuning

Numerical stability issues inadequately addressed: backpropagation through inverse covariance matrix (Section 4) noted as unstable; workaround (Eq. 5) requires solving optimization over ω but convergence and numerical stability not analyzed
Sample splitting reduces effective sample size compared to single-dataset methods; computational cost comparison to SpecIV not provided
Iterative OPE procedure (Section E.7.2) lacks convergence analysis; potential for dynamic spectral misalignment identified but not formally analyzed

Key result (Theorem C.6 on approximation error) relegated to appendix; main text lacks intuition for why augmentation 'amplifies' misaligned components; error bounds scale as λ_k^{-2} for bad scenario, becoming loose for small singular values

strengths: Clearly identifies and addresses a genuine limitation of SpecIV (spectral misalignment) with well-motivated examples
Rigorous theoretical analysis including non-asymptotic error bounds, detailed perturbation analysis, and characterization of 'good' vs 'bad' scenarios
Elegant connection between outcome-aware loss function and rank-d approximation of augmented operator T_δ (Proposition 4.1)
Well-designed experiments with new challenging dSprites benchmark (h_new) and substantial empirical improvements
Demonstrates broader applicability beyond IV to off-policy evaluation in reinforcement learning
Honest treatment of limitations and gaps between theory and practice (e.g., DNN optimization, hyperparameter selection)
weaknesses: Unresolved gap between theory (assuming exact SVD of T_δ) and practice (approximate neural network training) - acknowledged but not addressed
Hyperparameter δ selection lacks principled guidance; proposed methods are somewhat ad-hoc (5% improvement heuristic, stage-2 loss minimization without theoretical justification)
Analysis restricted to rank-one augmentation; higher-rank extensions incomplete and show minimal additional benefits
Missing convergence rate characterization for representation learning error as function of sample size m
Limited empirical comparison to related adaptive methods (Bruns-Smith 2025) and other outcome-aware IV approaches
OPE experiments show modest improvements compared to IV benchmarks and no uniform advantage across tasks
